practicalQuestion: During a seven-day travel period with two competitions, limited food access, and athletes with different playing-time demands, how should performance nutrition prioritize and individualize fueling, hydration, recovery, and supplement decisions while protecting sleep and gastrointestinal tolerance?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes
decisionContext.outcome: Create an operational nutrition plan that supports readiness across subgroups
decisionContext.constraints: Fixed travel and hotel meals; limited refrigeration; variable minutes and sweat response; supplement and clinical decisions require appropriate review

evidenceConfidence.rationale: Two independent expert sources, the UEFA football nutrition statement and a rugby league review, give direct but general guidance on carbohydrate, protein, fluids, gut comfort, food hygiene, sports foods away from home and supplement caution. No source tests the decision this question asks about: individualizing a travel-week nutrition plan by playing minutes in collegiate athletes. Most numbers come from male professional rugby league or football, small laboratory studies or a two-player case study. A hydration meta-analysis found no significant pooled glycogen difference with rehydration, and that tension is not resolved for this context. The tier is therefore Limited, and the steps below are options, not a recommended plan.

dimensions.sourceReview: Sources are an expert consensus statement in elite football, a narrative review in young professional male rugby league, systematic reviews and meta-analyses on hydration and glycogen, caffeine, melatonin and antioxidants, a two-player case study in elite Australian Football, observational studies on match minutes and travel, and one small randomized crossover nap trial.
dimensions.directness: Fueling, recovery, hydration and sports-food guidance is direct but general. No source tests how to individualize nutrition by playing minutes during a congested travel week, or how to build plans around fixed hotel meals. Sleep evidence covers travel and naps, not how nutrition choices affect sleep.
dimensions.consistency: Fueling and recovery guidance points the same way across the two expert sources, although their pre-competition ranges and timings differ slightly. The hydration and glycogen evidence is mixed: the review authors' practical interpretation favors full rehydration, but their pooled analysis did not show a significant glycogen difference, and the UEFA statement notes normal eating and drinking usually restores fluid balance.
dimensions.transferability: Populations are mostly professional or elite male soccer, rugby league, rugby union and Australian Football players, plus laboratory samples of mostly male trained or recreational adults and trained youth males. The caffeine and antioxidant meta-analyses included some women. The UEFA statement notes few studies in women's football. Transfer to a mixed-sex collegiate roster with returning athletes is uncertain.

bottomLine.text: The evidence supports a food-first base for the whole squad: carbohydrate-focused meals that are easy to digest, planned fluid and electrolyte intake, safe food handling, and sports foods as a backup when meals away from home fall short. Expert guidance for congested schedules suggests keeping carbohydrate at about 6 to 8 g/kg per day around each competition and for 48 to 72 hours after it. No source tests adjusting this base by playing minutes, so any subgroup layer is professional judgment. Supplements and sleep aids belong with medical, dietetic and compliance review. The cited ranges come mostly from male professional collision and football codes, so treat them as starting points to adjust, not targets.

actions.title: Option: anchor carbohydrate around both competitions
actions.text: The UEFA statement suggests a carbohydrate-rich meal of 1 to 3 g/kg 3 to 4 hours before kick-off, within an overall 6 to 8 g/kg per day, and keeping 6 to 8 g/kg per day for up to 48 to 72 hours after a match during congested schedules. The rugby league review, written for 80 to 120 kg players, suggests 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 g/kg protein 1 to 4 hours before competition, and 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 to 0.55 g/kg protein within 0 to 2 hours after. That review notes the post-exercise carbohydrate amount depends on whether rapid glycogen restoration is the priority, which matters most if game two follows soon after game one. The hydration review cites earlier laboratory work reporting that, with about 1 to 1.2 g/kg carbohydrate per hour, about 40% of glycogen can be restored in the first hour and about 75% within 4 to 5 hours.

actions.title: Option: consider playing minutes, with caution
actions.text: In one professional soccer team, players with more match playing time had higher accumulated weekly external load for most variables. In that same team, players who played under 60 minutes, including those who did not play, completed a next-day compensatory session meant to reproduce competitive loads. In a two-player case study, the player who took carbohydrate gels during play used less glycogen, but also played fewer minutes, so fueling and workload are confounded. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): offer high-minute athletes the fuller recovery ranges and an in-game carbohydrate option they have already tolerated, and match low-minute athletes' carbohydrate to the training they actually complete, including any compensatory session, rather than cutting it by default.

actions.title: Option: individualize fluids and electrolytes
actions.text: Sweat rates vary greatly between players, so one fluid plan will not fit everyone. The UEFA statement suggests 5 to 7 mL/kg of fluid in the 2 to 4 hours before kick-off. In its hot-environment section, for when specialist support is not possible, it recommends ample fluids and foods high in sodium, potassium and water, plus a morning self-check of body weight and thirst. After a match it advises reducing any fluid and electrolyte deficit soon, while noting that in most situations normal eating and drinking gives enough time to restore balance. The hydration review authors suggest poor rehydration may hurt performance over consecutive days, but their pooled analysis did not confirm the glycogen mechanism.

actions.title: Option: protect gut tolerance, food access and food safety
actions.text: The UEFA statement says the pre-match meal should be easily digestible and comfortable for the player, rather than following rigid intake strategies alone. It notes that sports foods can be a preferred way to supply carbohydrate when appetite is reduced or food is sourced away from home, and that carbohydrate drinks and gels can help where fear or experience of gastrointestinal problems limits intake during matches. For illness risk it highlights food hygiene focused on cross-contamination, cleaning, chilling and cooking. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with fixed hotel meals and limited refrigeration, pack shelf-stable carbohydrate and protein options that athletes have already tolerated in training.

actions.title: Option: route supplements and sleep aids through review
actions.text: The UEFA statement says the evidence for caffeine and creatine is stronger than for some other performance supplements, and that supplements should be trialled and monitored in training before competition use. A caffeine meta-analysis found a significant ergogenic effect at under 3 and at 3 to 6 mg/kg, but not above 6 mg/kg. The rugby league review cautions about possible side effects such as sleep disturbances and anxiety, and cites earlier work giving a caffeine half-life of about 2.5 to 10 hours. A melatonin meta-analysis found no effect on aerobic or strength performance. A Cochrane review found high-dose antioxidant supplements did not give a clinically relevant reduction in muscle soreness, and the UEFA statement discourages large doses of vitamins C and E. Team-wide supplement use calls for extreme caution because of team-level anti-doping consequences. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): weigh caffeine timing against sleep, especially for evening competitions.

monitoring.label: Morning hydration check
monitoring.text: Option: each morning, have athletes record body weight and thirst, a self-check the UEFA statement suggests in hot conditions when specialist support is not available. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): use the results to adjust fluid and sodium for athletes whose losses differ from the group.

monitoring.label: Recovery window between competitions
monitoring.text: The UEFA statement notes elite players may not reach carbohydrate targets in recovery from evening games. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): check whether high-minute athletes actually eat the post-competition carbohydrate and protein in the first hours after game one.

monitoring.label: Sleep and travel fatigue
monitoring.text: The UEFA statement reports reduced performance for up to 72 hours after long-haul travel across time zones, with severity tied to time zones crossed and cumulative sleep loss, and lists adequate recovery and sleep among illness-risk measures. In professional male rugby union players, the authors recommend arriving more than 3 days before matches after overnight long-haul travel. In national-team footballers, daytime arrivals (11 AM to 5 PM) went with better perceptual responses than early-morning or late-night arrivals. In trained youth male athletes after a normal night's sleep, a 90-minute nap at 13:00 helped some outcomes more than a 15:00 nap or no nap, and the authors advise testing nap timing on each athlete before use.

monitoring.label: Gut comfort
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): record gastrointestinal complaints after pre-competition meals and in-game fueling, and adjust food choices for the athletes affected.

guardrails.text: Supplement, sleep-aid and other clinical decisions stay with the appropriate medical, dietetic and compliance review. The UEFA statement warns that whole-team supplement use calls for extreme caution, because violations by three or more players can lead to team disqualification. It also says pharmacological sleep interventions, such as melatonin for jet lag, should be overseen by a medical doctor, with sleep hygiene considered first.

The UEFA rehabilitation guidance includes avoiding drastic cuts in energy intake and a daily protein intake of at least 1.6 g/kg, spread as 20 to 30 g leucine-rich doses. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): returning athletes' nutrition targets, training progression and clearance decisions stay with their treating clinicians. This brief does not set their targets.

The numeric ranges come from expert guidance in male professional rugby league and football and from laboratory studies. The rugby league review authors note there may not be enough data for sport-specific recommendations. Do not apply them as fixed prescriptions.

limitations.text: Most evidence comes from male professional or elite athletes in rugby league, rugby union, Australian Football and soccer. The UEFA statement notes there is little research specific to football and few studies in women's football. No source studies collegiate or female athletes during travel.
The in-game fueling evidence is a two-player case study in which fueling and minutes played were confounded.
The antioxidant review included no data from highly trained elite athletes. The nap trial studied trained youth males only.

whatCouldChange.text: Studies that test carbohydrate or recovery plans individualized by playing minutes in collegiate or female team-sport athletes could firm up or change the subgroup layer.
Larger randomized trials of in-game carbohydrate feeding, which the case study authors call for, could strengthen or weaken the high-minute fueling option.

Research on whether players can meet carbohydrate targets while traveling for away games, which the rugby league review calls for, could change how much the plan relies on sports foods and packed options.
Clearer evidence on whether rehydration changes glycogen recovery could change how strongly rehydration is prioritized between the two competitions.

evidenceTension.text: The hydration and glycogen review authors say poor rehydration may increase glycogen use in the next session and hurt performance over consecutive days. However, their own pooled analysis of 10 studies found no significant glycogen difference between rehydrated and dehydrated conditions, with very high heterogeneity, and they cite earlier work in which water deprivation did not hinder glycogen resynthesis over 15 hours. The UEFA statement adds that normal eating and drinking usually gives enough time to restore fluid balance after a match. Rehydration remains a sensible priority between games, but the glycogen mechanism is uncertain, and this tension is not resolved for a two-game travel week.

assumptions: The number of time zones crossed and the flight timing are unknown, so the jet lag and long-haul travel findings may apply only partly.
'Returning athletes' is read as athletes returning from injury or reduced training, whose plans involve their treating clinicians.
Athlete body mass, sex mix, competition start times and environmental heat are unknown, so per-kilogram ranges must be converted individually.
The spacing between the two competitions is unknown. Post-competition ranges aimed at rapid glycogen restoration matter most if game two follows within a few days.
coverageGaps: No source tests nutrition plans individualized by playing minutes (high-minute, low-minute or non-playing athletes) during a congested week.
No travel nutrition evidence in collegiate or female athletes.

No source tests plans built around fixed hotel meals or limited refrigeration. The pack offers only food hygiene principles, sports foods as an option when food is sourced away from home, and a rugby league call for research on meeting carbohydrate targets when traveling.
No source tests how caffeine timing before evening competition affects athlete sleep. Sources only flag sleep disturbance as a possible side effect and give a half-life range from earlier work.

The pack has general UEFA injury rehabilitation nutrition guidance but no evidence on travel-week nutrition for athletes returning from injury or reduced training. The creatine during sleep deprivation lead (libraryId 613) has no accessible text.
